name: ESP-01
description: Compact ESP8266-based 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi module on a 2x4 header, the smallest popular ESP8266 board. It can run as a UART-to-Wi-Fi bridge via AT-command firmware or be reprogrammed with custom firmware (Arduino core, NodeMCU/Lua, MicroPython). It exposes only two usable GPIOs (GPIO0 and GPIO2) plus the UART. It is strictly a 3.3 V part - VCC and all logic are 3.3 V, not 5 V tolerant - and the radio draws high current spikes that demand a solid 3.3 V supply.

pins.name: GPIO2
pins.description: GPIO2; must be high at boot; usable as I/O after boot

pins.name: GPIO0
pins.description: GPIO0; pull LOW at boot to enter flash/programming mode, high for normal run

pins.name: CH_PD
pins.description: chip enable / power-down; tie HIGH (to 3.3 V) to run

pins.name: RST
pins.description: active-low reset; high for normal operation

pins.name: VCC
pins.description: 3.3 V supply (NOT 5 V tolerant); high peak current

typical_application: Adding Wi-Fi to a microcontroller over UART (AT commands), or as a standalone tiny Wi-Fi IoT node when reflashed with custom firmware.
gotchas: 3.3 V ONLY on VCC and all logic; a 5 V supply or 5 V UART lines will destroy the module - level shift a 5 V MCU's TX into RXD
the onboard 3.3 V regulator on many host boards cannot supply the ~300-400 mA TX bursts; brownouts cause resets/Wi-Fi failures - use a dedicated 3.3 V regulator with bulk capacitance
boot strapping: CH_PD high, RST high, GPIO0 high for normal run; GPIO0 LOW at reset enters flash mode - getting these wrong means it won't boot
GPIO2 must not be held low at boot or the module fails to start
only two GPIOs are broken out, so the ESP-01 is I/O-limited; use a larger ESP board if you need more pins
the bare 2x4 header is easy to misorient; confirm pin 1 against the silkscreen
